chunks: From him, from Safwan and Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil, from Zurarah, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:
"A camel for two camels, and a beast of burden for two beasts of burden, hand-to-hand (on the spot), there is no objection to it."

key_terms.الدَّابَّةُ: A beast of burden (e.g., donkey, horse, camel)
key_terms.الْبَعِيرُ: A camel (specifically a female camel used for milk or riding, often used generically for camel in trade contexts)
key_terms.لَيْسَ بِهِ بَأْسٌ: There is no objection to it; it is permissible
key_terms.يَدًا بِيَدٍ: Hand-to-hand; a spot transaction with immediate exchange and no delay

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to trade one camel for two camels in Islamic law?
ai.summary: Recorded in Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* within the chapter on *Bay'*, this hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that exchanging one animal for two of the same species is permissible in a spot transaction (*yadan bi-yad*), provided the items are of the same genus. This ruling distinguishes such exchanges from *Riba al-Fadl* by emphasizing the immediate nature of the trade, a key principle in Shia jurisprudence for validating commodity swaps without interest. The chain of transmission through Zurarah and Jamil underscores the reliability of this legal precedent in early Shia hadith literature.
